The shameless Phariseeism of these smug little guardians of humanitarian virtue!
Rousseau stands at the beginning of all such lies.
But at least he himself was still a poor tormented devil, a helpless bohemian.
Now, by contrast, along come the fat, overfed gluttons and declare our starving corpses morally disgusting.
I do not barricade myself inside a conclusion.
I do not bury myself in an achievement.
That means I do not die and I do not look backward.
I continue to serve, and therefore I continue to live.
I do not stop at any thought.
I do not remain with any conclusion.
I keep going and keep pushing onward.
That is why only a few people can follow me.
They stop at some particular point in my process of thought and try to pin me down there.
In other words, they declare me dead because they themselves are dead.
They want to fix me in place and make me rigid, just as they themselves are fixed and rigid.
Anyone who wants to hold me to my <yesterday’s> thought will find that I am already in the beyond.
I have disappeared into what cannot be grasped.
And this is why they become furious when they discover that physically I am still alive, however modestly and secretly, somewhere in some miserable refuge.
Their desire to persecute me bursts into flame at the thought that I am still alive not only intellectually, but physically as well.
These people belong to the past.
For that reason they are dead.
But they do not know death.
I have known it for a long time.
It is constantly reborn from the spirit and from thought: life as the great festival of , in whose constant transformation physical death is only one moment among many.
I have already died many times.
As for what there is to fear in physical death, and what there is not to fear, I have considerable experience.

I fear physical death less than I fear the filthy meanness of those shades who tried to drag me down onto the level of their own corpses: those poor fat caterpillars trying to glue a butterfly in flight with their slime.

How charmingly she speaks, in her language and her surroundings: a girl; a bright and intelligent, wisely foolish virgin; one could imagine nothing more beautiful.
Then she falls in love twice.
Each time with a bourgeois literary man who probably won her heart only because he offered her the literary understanding she could not find among people of her own estate, class, and caste.
But they never reached the core of her being.
An intelligent girl, intelligent even in a practical domestic sense.
In an age that was coming apart, she remained unstupid, indestructible right down to the heart.
And yet she was obedient, as every good woman was expected to be, obedient to her time.
She went along with its currents.
She dutifully participated in the literary business of her age.
At times she verses together in a Schillerian , in the of this <…> and of this dissolved Lenau.
The doubts of The Spiritual Year are the recoil back into herself after those foolish infatuations with literary men.
Her accusations against herself become so terrible because she carries a great standard within herself.
At the beginning of the age of l’art pour l’art, she certainly participates in the literary world—but no more than is proper for a well-brought-up, respectable, obedient girl.
At the deepest level she knows the nihilism of her age.
That is the meaning of The Spiritual Year.

The sadness of not being saints.
